questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Other

questions.question: Please explain: *
questions.answer: Mandatory exchange for students of Japan Studies of one semester (Sep.-Dec. 2025)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Seinan Gakuin University had many interesting courses on offer, including joint courses with the Japanese students. The courses on offer and overall course system were changed shortly after our referrals, however, to emphasize said joint courses more. Another determining factor for me was the possibility for special academic support, and at a smaller academic institution, due to my disabilities. The English version of their website was also highly informative and easy to navigate compared to those of others, and held detailed information on all the practicalities. Lastly, my former Japanese teacher highly recommended both the university and Fukuoka, citing their own positive experiences there.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was very happy with my host university and exchange stay overall. The university staff at Seinan and my professors were patient, helpful and accomodating, and I enjoyed the courses a lot - but I do know of some who had less fortunate experiences with their professors. Fukuoka was highly livable, and the dorms being right by our campus provided a convenient home base without any need for public transport to and from classes or nearby stores. However, due to events in my personal life leading to a lacking social network while abroad, the stay itself became difficult to manage. Namely due to my relatively low Japanese proficiency level. Similarly, I also felt woefully underprepared in terms of the language level, as all of our language classes were held in Japanese. By comparison, our Japanese classes at the University of Copenhagen (UCPH) were largely held in Danish compared to the language classes of other area studies, such as Korea Studies.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: The university staff were very thorough in mailing us guides and timely information both before and upon arrival. Much of the information was already available on the university's website as well, and the Center for International Education (CIE) was open for drop-ins during opening hours.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: A week-long joint orientation was held for all international students, followed by meeting our assigned student helpers of the local Japanese student body to show us around and answer questions. Said assigned helpers also assisted us with the necessary procedures at the local ward office. Furthermore, as we were to move into our respective dormitories 1-2 days before the orientation, we were given a thorough rundown of the different rules of our dormitory upon arrival, such as quiet hour after 22:00 (23:00 on weekends), no smoking or consuming alcohol inside the dorms, cleaning duty, safety precautions, special rules for bicycles, et cetera. The Japanese dorm managers and student RAs kindly helped us settle in and move our luggage to our respective rooms.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: The orientation was very in-depth and included plenty of help with setting up our intranet user profiles, necessary paperwork for the ward office procedures (signing up for a Japanese bank account was not required), et cetera. The orientation also included a fun field trip to local sights for all international students. I was also immensely grateful for the special academic support I was able to receive even before arriving in Japan, and the opportunity to meet and get to know the Japanese students in a cooperative way was greatly appreciated. That being said, as we were seemingly assigned student helpers based on our Japanese proficiency level test scores, and my scores were for reasons unknown far above my actual level, I unfortunately struggled immensely with communicating despite my assigned helper's always kind and patient efforts to bridge the language gap. To avoid burdening them with too much extra work, I often went to the CIE for assistance instead.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Aside from the option for co-ed or female-only off-campus housing via Kyoritsu and Dormy Fukuoka, the university also offered three on-campus dormitories: two co-ed (Minato and Hekiha) and one female only (Migiwa). Information and price estimates were listed in detail on Seinan's website.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: All on-campus dorms required students to cook for themselves in the respective communal kitchens - however, the on-campus cafeteria offered various customizable lunch and evening meals. The off-campus dorms included breakfast and dinner meal plans.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Minato and Migiwa had communal showers or baths, whereas Hekiha offered private en suite baths. Migiwa also had a mix of individual and double rooms. Students were asked to list their highest to lowest priority among the available options, including the options for individual or double rooms in the case of Migiwa. There was no curfew, but visitors were only allowed in the communal spaces and after signing a paper - in Migiwa, female family members were allowed into the rooms. Guests had to leave by 22 o'clock at the latest. Smoking and alcohol consumption was prohibited inside the dorms. If special support was required, such as in the case of disabilities, this was also taken into account - although I was assigned a double room in Migiwa, my lowest priority, they had kindly arranged for me to not have a roommate in order to accomodate my situation. Regarding cleaning, all dormitories had mandatory daily and weekly cleaning duties distributed among tenants. Outside of this, students were also expected to clean up after themselves with plenty of instructions hung up to ease the process. Despite this, these rules were in many cases ignored by a number of tenants in Migiwa, despite multiple warnings, leading to unpleasant conditions in the kitchen and shower rooms especially. Don't be that person.

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The on-campus housing was very affordable (in the 38.000-48.000 yen range), conveniently close to our campus, various grocery stores, shopping streets and restaurants, and well connected with various bus lines and the city subway close by. Each room also had WiFi. My only gripe was the conditions that other students would leave the communal spaces of our dormitory in. If you have respiratory problems, see if you can arrange for checking whether the airconditioning unit in your room is decently clean. Also, given the humid environment, the dehumidifying option is a lifesaver if your clothing cannot be tumbledried.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Seinan offers two course plans: Plan A, which is Japanese language focused - and Plan B for those who have limited or no experience with Japanese and is thus electives focused. The course registration process in itself was easy to follow - however, the wording 'select at least one' led to some confusion. I was under the impression that we were to apply for the courses we would ideally like, then choose between the ones available to us by designation or lottery. This was not the case. Hence, I ended up with too many courses, and the recently added mandatory Global Liberal Arts (GLA) joint courses could not be dropped. Furthermore, as previously mentioned the course system had been recently changed by the time we arrived, meaning it was quite new to everyone and still being optimized.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The Japanese language courses were registered according to individual Japanese placement test results and history of Japanese language study. The placement test itself was based on the TTBJ test. No interview or the like was required. Furthermore, it was possible to be moved to a higher or lower level after the initial assessment during the first week. The elective courses were split into two groups: mandatory GLA joint courses alongside the Japanese students, and regular elective courses within the international division plus special topic courses offered in the regular department. The registration process was done via two separate online forms requiring one's name, e-mail address, curriculum plan (A or B), and one's courses of choice from the given list. First was the GLA courses, then the second group of electives. In case of exceeded capacity, the spots were distributed by lottery. Re-registration was similarly done via an online form. Dropping courses was done by crossing out the course(s) in question on the printed handout and handing it in at the CIE before the given deadline.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Detailed information about the course contents for each course was available on university's official website. The CIE were also very helpful with any and all questions I had regarding the course registration, options in case of overlapping courses, the possibility of self-studying courses that were moved form the Fall semester to the Spring semester, et cetera.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Given my misunderstanding of the wording on the course registration form, I ended up with too many courses as I managed to get into every course I applied for - including two undroppable GLA joint courses. In this sense, I was successful in registering for every class I wanted. However, many of the courses I was originally interested in were moved from the Fall semester to the Spring semester due to the recent introduction of the GLA courses. Hence, I also had to make do with the courses that remained.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be sure to check the most up-to-date course catalogue on the website, and be mindful of which courses are Fall semester courses and which are Spring. Also be mindful that it is only mandatory to take one GLA course and that registering for more in case of not getting a spot may backfire, as they could not be dropped. For the electives, I recommend going for what sounds most interesting or relevant to you or your desired specialization. Despite being a smaller, private institution, Seinan offers a wide variety of subjects from arts, history, culture and religion, to sociology, business, politics and law, national sports, the natural world of Japan, and even manga and anime-focused communications- and societal studies. I also recommend checking out the special topic courses - many were in English as well. Seinan also offered tandem learning with Japanese students on agreed-upon subjects, as well as independent study.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Although I wish a few of my classes had gone a bit more in depth, I was satisfied with the academic programme and found it appropriate overall for an international division of mixed students with very different backgrounds, reasons for studying there, and linguistic proficiency in both Japanese and English. The opportunity to have classes alongside the Japanese students was both intimidating and fun, and many were able to make new friends this way.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The elective courses seemed appropriately difficult while also being mindful of the different levels of English among both professors and students, particularly professors who had no prior experience of teaching entire courses in English. Note, however, that the Japanese level IV courses were of pre-intermediate level, i.e. N4-N3, rather than level III. The GLA courses were less demanding in order to accomodate the Japanese students, as said courses were held entirely in English. Another important reason for any seemingly lower level is that the university years for Japanese students are mainly spent job hunting, meaning less time for classes and thus a different approach to university-level education as a whole.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: I found the style of teaching at Seinan more pedagogical than what I have experienced at the UCPH thus far. Mainly due to the emphasis on summarizing each class at the end of class, setting aside time for taking notes, practical application of what was gained from each class in shorter assignments or presentations, and more. However, each class was also 100 minutes long and usually without breaks. This allows for more time for discussions, spreading out and summarizing information, et cetera - but it can also be quite tough to remain focused for so long. Japanese levels II and above had two classes in the mornings four days a week, i.e. 200 minutes in total in a day - add to that the weekly elective courses.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Aside from Japanese level IV language courses, I was enrolled in GLA Psychology, GLA Culture, Japanese Business Culture, and Special Topic: English for Specific Purposes (a social linguistics course). Despite a few changes to the course contents, I was happy with all of them. Although, I was sad to drop Japanese History due to unexpected course overlap.

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I recommend every elective course I took. Our Japanese Business Culture professor made the course very engaging by drawing lively comparisons different business cultures and including the students in discussions of the class material throughout - the final project involved adapting a Japanese product or service to one's domestic market or vice versa. Psychology taught me a lot about the differences between our idea of concepts such as health, happiness, learning, orientation, habits, et cetera versus Japanese views, as well as how much of our modern psychology is increasingly similar to East Asian philosophies. Culture provided many insights into not only Japanese culture and history from a Japanese perspective, but also those of other cultures through comparative group discussions and short presentations. Finally, English for Specific Purposes gave a great view into what language is in relation to culture and society, and what linguistic differences reflect and affect in terms of how we view and communicate our world and experiences. That being said, in hindsight I wish I had taken GLA Politics and Law to fill the gap in my knowledge on both topics.

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I did a lot of research into insurance and eSim costs, rental fees, curricular materials, et cetera before traveling and thus did not end up encountering any unexpected costs. Seinan also has estimates for basic living expenses listed on their website. Books were 240 DKK in total, mandatory insurance in Japan 420 DKK in total, and eSim with voice and data enough for tethering 350 DKK a month. I did pay around 6.300 DKK for 4 months of travel insurance via Gouda only to find it did not cover one of my disabilities - the mandatory National Health Insurance in Japan may offer you better coverage as it covers 70 percent of medical expenses. Also, remember to always carry an amount of cash in case of an emergency, credit cards not working, et cetera.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Keep in mind that the cost of living in Japan is considerably lower than in Denmark - even the notorious fruit comes with plenty of affordable options. Despite my research prior to traveling, the low cost of living still shocked me, especially considering that many Japanese find it difficult to make ends meet - it truly put things into perspective as a student reliant on SU. Many things may be cheaper to buy in Japan than to bring along. I also bought far too many snacks for this reason, hence my high spending on food. Still, be aware that if you plan on traveling during your stay, long shinkansen trips may be expensive and low-cost alternatives such as overnight buses worth looking into. My handful of shinkansen trips account by far for most of my listed travel expenses - meanwhile, gifts for family and friends back home account for most of my personal spending. Other fees were mainly medicine, medical masks, cleaning products, gift wrapping, package mailing fees at the post office, and the like.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Despite being a smaller, private institution, Seinan offered a considerable amount of all kinds of non-academic opportunities. These range from sports (rugby, badminton, basketball, track and field, lacrosse, boating, and many more), martial arts (kyudo, kendo, shorinji-kenpo, and more), arts (painting, photography, calligraphy, tea ceremony), music, and social clubs, to events and parties arranged by local student groups. We were even invited to the university baseball team's games to cheer them on.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Seinan mails out information about events and clubs that are open to new members and international students. If any of them catch your interest, I recommend giving it a go, even if you may feel your language skills are not up to par. When engaging in something you are genuinely interested in, learning becomes much easier and more organic - while also providing an opportunity to hone your skills and meet new people along the way.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Do not be fooled by Kyushu's distance from places like Tokyo or Kyoto, as the island still has plenty to offer. The local area has everything from beautiful parks and beaches to mountains and caves, to lively shopping centers with 11-story department stores, famous temples and shrines, cozy rural areas, and even significant historical and archaeological sites relating to Japan's Yayoi period, the battles against the Mongols, and the eras of cultural exchange and uprisings against the shogun. Additionally, Japan's infrastructure is solid and trains do run on time, so even a day trip or weekend trip from Fukuoka can take you quite far. For those more interested in shopping, Fukuoka has lots of options, from alt fashion and niche stores to international brands, to entire stationary stores and manga and anime shops - even within the same department stores. Lastly, Fukuoka is in many ways famous for food, namely its yatai food stands, and has countless options for different cuisines. To name a few recommendations within Fukuoka, the genkoborui defensive wall at Iki-no-Matsubara beach, Nokonoshima island flower park, Dazaifu Tenmangu shrine dedicated students and learning, or one of the few one-to-one scale Gundam statues at Lalaport. For day trips, places like the two active volcanoes of Mt. Aso and Sakurajima, Keya no Oto cliff, Yoshinogari Historical Park, or the giant statues at Daihonzan Naritasan Kurume temple or Nanzo-in temple are definitely worth a visit. Okawachiyama and Kami-Arita's porcelain shrine in Saga are well worth a visit for anyone interested in porcelain, and Huis Ten Bosch in Nagasaki has a spectacular fireworks show in November. You could also make weekend trips to places further away, such as Okinawa, the Shimanami Kaido, or even other East Asian countries (if permitted by your visa).

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: After many years of interest in Japan, it was not too difficult to adjust to the local culture. Many things are not too different from behavioral norms in Denmark. Although Fukuoka is said to be more 'conservative' in terms of clothing, plenty wore alt fashion. Furthermore, Fukuoka has plenty of signage in English everywhere due to high tourism, and even stores are open until fairly late - one local supermarket was open 24 hours. Learning the basics of how to behave in public, on public transport, and during meals makes a good foundation. Though, mistakes are likely to happen when you inadvertently become flustered in an unfamiliar environment. If you ever feel unsure how to navigate a situation, there is no shame in asking. Alternatively, there are plenty of helpful guides online - and if all else fails, just remember that you are not expected to know every rule as an 'outsider'. And that translation software can be a lifesaver.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: As previously mentioned, Seinan offers many academic and non-academic opportunities to break the ice with local students, as many are curious but too shy to approach due to the language barrier. Just do your best, keep an open mind, and try not to pay too much mind to any mistakes - asking for recommendations often works too. You may even be invited to them.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I did not find the cultural differences difficult to navigate, but here are a few things to be mindful of aside from the language barrier. Talking on the phone or loudly among yourselves on public transport is frowned upon, though you will certainly find Japanese who do this as well. Jaywalking happens but is illegal, and people do wait in line and for traffic lights to turn green. Many international students also complained about all the necessary paperwork. Picking up on the subtle social cues may be challenging for those used to more open communication, and direct eye contact is still generally a social faux pas. For social, outgoing students, the fact that people tend to keep to themselves may also prove a challenge - for more introverted students, it may be challenging to feel that you always stand out, even when you try not to, and the high level of efficiency may make you feel like you are being a bother if you take too long. Lastly, while not a challenge relating to culture, the heat and high humidity was almost unbearable even in September when we arrived. We were told that this was uncommon, however, do be careful.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Personally, I appreciate the cultural emphasis on cleanliness, orderliness, and efficiency, and that it is socially acceptable to keep to yourself or go on solo trips. I also greatly appreciate the emphasis on how things are cared for and presented, especially food. That places like the ward office, post offices, and healthcare clinics had translation software or interpretation services available was a great help. And despite recent stories in the media about discontent with foreigners, I did not experience any unpleasantness myself - quite the opposite.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1. All deadlines are strict, and there are quite a lot of them initially and before returning home. The staff at Seinan were very generous with sending out reminders and thorough guides, but it may help to set reminders and divide each step into categories of urgent or not. 2. Do spend some time looking into not only the campus, dormitory options, and courses on offer, but also the area and what to pack depending on your plans. Especially in terms of dressing for the weather in both September and December. 3. Everyone I met at Seinan were very kind and accomodating, so do not be afraid to reach out if you need help. You are not alone.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Bear in mind that Seinan Gakuin University is a Christian university. That being said, while Christianity is still a core part of the university's background, Christian beliefs are by no means part of the curriculum, nor is there any dress code or punishment for alt fashion or the like, and religious freedom is of course in place.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The fact that I was able to complete a semester-long exchange far from home, despite my disabilities and the hurdles, felt immensely rewarding - particularly after many talks with the student counselors at UCPH about the possibility of not going. The kind of place that Fukuoka is, as well as the degree of accomodation at Seinan, certainly contributed to this.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Although I had studied Japanese for a year before enrolling in Japan Studies at the UCPH, the language barrier made me painfully aware of just how lacking my Japanese abilities are. It also kept me from doing many things, including eating out more.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Remember to look after yourself too. The Fall semester was tough, as classes had to be crammed into four months instead of five due to the structural changes. It is true that you are primarily going on an exchange to study - but (guilt-free!) breaks are also important to create an environment that is actually conducive to learning. 'Gakusei' should not be literal. So remember to be kind to yourself and that it is okay if there are things that cannot be done to a T. Don't be shy or ashamed if you have questions, the CIE, your student helper, and the dormitory managers and RAs are there to help. Seinan also has an English-speaking counselor if need be. There is no 'right' way - so just do what you can.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
